description: We’re two friends from Turkmenistan, now studying CS in the U.S.: Dovlet (Kent State) and Rahman (ASU). Rahman built an AI  surplus resale business, that scans auctions, values lots using real sold prices and recommends buy, watch or skip. He also researches diffusion models at ASU. Dovlet, a CS student with a Data Science minor, built the backend and data filtering for an ML platform matching sponsors with pro sports teams at KSU. We cover software, AI/ML, data analysis and data management.
summary: Rewind finds recently discovered asteroids and comets in older NASA SPHEREx images, taken before anyone knew they were there. These earlier detections are called precoveries. For each new object we compute where it was in the months before discovery, find every SPHEREx image that covered that spot, subtract the fixed sky, and stack the images along the object's predicted path. Nine checks decide whether a signal is real. We searched 265 objects in 19,130 SPHEREx images. Eight passed all nine checks, and seven of them were seen 4 to 20 days before their first known observation, including the potentially hazardous asteroids 2025 YH5 and 2025 ST20. A precovery adds a position from before discovery, so the object's future path becomes more certain: had Rewind run on discovery day, the one-year uncertainty of 2025 ST20 would have been about 6 times smaller (computed). Our public website lets anyone explore the results in 3D, view the real SPHEREx images, and check every number.
details:
What it does
When a new asteroid or comet is announced, its orbit rests on only a few days of observations. Rewind computes where the object was in the months before discovery, finds every NASA SPHEREx image that covered that spot, and checks whether the object is there.

How it works
1. Targets: 265 recently discovered asteroids and comets from the Minor Planet Center and JPL, plus lost objects and well-known controls.
2. Images: every SPHEREx Level 2 image that covers the predicted path, read from NASA's IRSA archive (19,130 images).
3. Clean: we subtract fixed stars and galaxies using other SPHEREx images of the same field.
4. Stack: we shift the image cutouts along the predicted path and add them up, so a faint moving object builds up while the noise averages out.
5. Checks: nine tests, including offset (null) paths, a time-shift test, single-day stacks, a sign test and planted test sources.
6. Verdict and orbit: an object is FOUND only when all nine checks pass. The new positions go into an orbit fit (kete) with the real MPC observations.

Results
265 objects searched; 8 FOUND; 7 of them 4 to 20 days before the first known observation (JPL SBDB); 48 HINT; 200 too faint; 7 with no SPHEREx coverage. 2025 YH5, a potentially hazardous asteroid, was imaged on 12 days, the first 18 days before discovery, and shows clearly when 81 images are stacked (S/N 34.4).

Testing
In a blind test on known objects with their later observations hidden, Rewind recovered 10 of 18 as FOUND, flagged 7 as HINT and missed 1, with 0 false FOUNDs in 23 real cases and 22 empty-sky decoys. Median position error 0.5 arcsec. The same code on a Mac and on Kaggle gave the same verdict for 12 of 12 objects.

Benefits and impact
Had Rewind run on discovery day, our positions would have made the one-year position uncertainty about 6 times smaller for 2025 ST20 (16 to 2.7 million km) and about 3 times smaller for 2025 YH5 (3.5 to 1.1 million km). These are computed scenarios. Today, after months of follow-up, the same positions change the orbits by only 0 to 7 percent, so the value is speed right after discovery.

Limits
The finds are stack-only, have not been reported to the Minor Planet Center and are not peer-reviewed. On 15 Nov 2026 we checked all 455 objects found since 1 Nov; the 12 we could measure were too faint, because the public SPHEREx images end about six weeks before today.

The website
A 3D solar system with all 265 objects; a page for each object with its SPHEREx images, checks, spectrum and orbit; a Sky images page that reads SPHEREx pixels live from NASA's archive for any position; three short games on real data; and a Methods page with every data file, the checks, the blind test and our positions in MPC format. Slides: https://rewind.up.railway.app/media/Rewind-slides.pdf

Tools
Python (astropy, numpy, kete, sbpy, photutils), TypeScript, Vite and three.js, Kaggle notebooks for the large runs, Railway for hosting. Code: https://github.com/d-gurbano/nasa-space-x

Use of AI
We wrote the code with the help of Claude Code (Anthropic), an AI coding assistant, and reviewed, ran and tested it.
